claims.text: The starting material is the HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy has a quasi-static yield strength of 786 MPa.
The starting alloy has a quasi-static compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The starting alloy has a quasi-static fracture strain of 13.5%.
The proposed intervention is the addition of approximately 2 at.% Nb to HfZrTiTa0.53.
Adding approximately 2 at.% Nb will produce nanoscale Nb-rich precipitates in situ during processing.
The nanoscale Nb-rich precipitates will be finely dispersed within the alloy microstructure.
The Nb-rich particles will obstruct dislocation motion.
The precipitates will enhance dislocation interactions and dynamic strain hardening.
Enhanced dynamic strain hardening will retard adiabatic shear-band development and delay strain localization.
Delayed localization will extend uniform plastic deformation and delay rapid dynamic failure.
Under dynamic loading, the Nb-modified alloy will have approximately 10–15% higher yield and compressive strength than the baseline.
The Nb-modified alloy will improve uniform deformability by approximately 15–20% relative to the baseline.
The Nb-modified alloy will improve resistance to strain localization by approximately 15–20% relative to the baseline.
The Nb-modified alloy will distribute impact-induced energy release more gradually over a longer deformation period.
The predicted improvements apply primarily to adiabatic dynamic deformation at strain rates of approximately 10^3–10^4 s^-1.
Effects of the Nb addition under quasi-static loading are uncertain.
Approximately 2 at.% Nb may not be the optimum Nb concentration.

contradictions.description: The prediction is framed as more gradual impact-induced energy release, whereas the experiment measures energy absorption from the stress–strain curve; these are not necessarily equivalent observables, so the proposed measurement does not directly test the stated energy-release outcome.
